title: Euclid’s view of spiral galaxy IC 342
caption: The spiral galaxy IC 342, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: IC 342, Caldwell 5, the “Hidden Galaxy” · constellation Camelopardalis · about 10.7 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: One of Euclid’s first five full-color images (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A spiral galaxy spreads across this Euclid image, seen through a curtain of foreground stars. This is IC 342, also known as Caldwell 5, about 10.7 million light-years away in Camelopardalis, the Giraffe.

It is nicknamed the “Hidden Galaxy” because it sits behind the busy disc of our own Milky Way, where dust, gas and stars get in the way. That makes it hard to study in visible light. Euclid’s near-infrared instrument could see through much of the dust and measure the light of the galaxy’s many cooler, low-mass stars, which make up most of its mass.

The image took about an hour of observing. Over its lifetime Euclid will photograph billions of galaxies to reveal the unseen influence of dark matter and dark energy on them, so a galaxy hidden behind our own was a fitting early target.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 10.7 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 130,000 × 130,000 light-years. Its light set out about 10.7 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: In Euclid’s colors, hot stars appear white-blue, glowing hydrogen blue, and dusty, gas-rich regions red. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
